name: One system. Four routes.
what: A pump sends water to four upper channels. Each upper channel connects to one lower channel. The four returns combine into a single line back to the reservoir.
why: The pump lifts the water; the channel slopes and connections are intended to let gravity carry it back. The animation shows direction only—not measured speed or equal flow.
look: Choose a part of the model or use the component list below.

name: A structure to build on
what: The timber frame supports two levels of growing channels and the lights above them. Diagonal braces connect the upright and horizontal members.
why: Bracing helps a rectangular frame resist sideways distortion. The casters let the classroom structure be repositioned.
look: The proportions are estimated from the photos; this model is not a structural plan.

name: Where the loop begins
what: The reservoir holds the water supply and receives the combined return. Later, it will hold the nutrient solution used by the plants.
why: A shared reservoir allows water to circulate through the system again. Its final capacity and operating level are still to be confirmed.
look: The open view reveals a schematic pump. The real reservoir cover and plumbing details may differ.

name: Give water a lift
what: A submerged pump moves water from the reservoir up to the supply line.
why: The pump transfers energy to the water so it can rise above the reservoir. Actual flow depends on the pump, lift height, tubing, and fittings.
look: The planning lists name different pump ratings. The installed model and flow rate have not been confirmed.

name: One becomes four
what: T-shaped fittings branch the pump’s single supply line into four feeds—one for each upper channel.
why: Each simple tee can add one outlet. A branching tree needs three tees to turn one inlet into four outlets. Branch resistance can differ, so splitting does not guarantee equal flow.
look: Trace a single route with the 1–4 buttons. Fitting locations and tube diameters remain illustrative.

name: The first growing level
what: Four white channels hold planting sites. Water is intended to travel along each upper channel before moving to its matching lower channel.
why: Hydroponics supplies roots with water and dissolved mineral nutrients. Roots also need oxygen; the final water depth and aeration approach still need testing.
look: The planning list specifies 3-inch pipe for this level. Hole count and spacing in the model are approximate.

name: A pair, not a waterfall
what: Each upper channel connects only to the lower channel directly paired with it. The four routes stay separate between levels.
why: The change in height allows gravity to carry water toward the lower level. The exact connections, slopes, and drainage will be tested during the build.
look: Upper channel 1 feeds lower channel 1; the same pairing continues for routes 2, 3, and 4.

name: The second growing level
what: The turquoise channels receive water from their matching upper channels and carry it toward the return fittings.
why: This arrangement places two growing channels in each route. Observations will help us see whether water moves reliably through both levels.
look: The planning list specifies 4-inch pipe here. No planting or harvest results are being claimed yet.

name: Four become one again
what: The four lower-channel outlets join through tees into one return line leading back to the reservoir.
why: This completes the circulation loop. The combined return must drain the incoming water without backing up; its size and venting still need to be determined.
look: The diagram explains the topology. It does not establish that a particular tube size can handle the combined flow.

name: Light for a living system
what: Lights are mounted above both growing levels, where plants will eventually sit in the channels.
why: Light supplies energy for photosynthesis. The classroom can investigate how placement and duration affect growth once plants are established.
look: The model uses a soft pink tint to echo the lighting in the reference photos.
